title: Arrays and objects
intro: Real applications rarely work with one value at a time: a webshop has products, a cart has multiple items, and a booking system has lists of reservations. In this lesson, you will learn how arrays and objects work together and how to transform data safely without accidentally changing the original values.
takeaways: Objects represent structured entities while arrays represent ordered collections of values.
Use map, filter, find, some, every and reduce according to the kind of operation you need.
sort mutates the original array, so copy an array first when you need to preserve it.
Destructuring and spread make it easier to read values and create new arrays or objects without direct mutation.
JSON.stringify and JSON.parse convert between JavaScript values and the JSON text commonly exchanged with APIs.

quiz.question: What does `map()` normally return?
options: The first matching item
A new array containing the transformed items
A boolean
The original array after sorting
quiz.explanation: map() calls its callback for each item and creates a new array from the callback results.

quiz.question: What does this expression return? `cart.filter(item => item.price > 100)`
options: The first item costing more than 100
The number of expensive items
A new array containing items costing more than 100
A boolean indicating whether an expensive item exists
quiz.explanation: filter() creates a new array containing every item for which the callback returns true.

quiz.question: Which statement about `sort()` is correct?
options: It always returns a completely independent copy
It can only sort strings
It never changes the original array
It mutates the array and can receive a compare function
quiz.explanation: sort() changes the array it is called on. A compare function such as (a, b) => a - b is commonly used for numeric sorting.

quiz.question: What does this code produce? `const { name, price } = product;`
options: Variables named name and price containing matching properties from product
A new array containing product properties
A JSON string
A copy of product with only name and price
quiz.explanation: Object destructuring extracts properties from an object into variables with the corresponding names.

quiz.question: Which expression creates a new array containing all elements of `cart` followed by `newItem`?
options: cart.push(newItem)
cart + newItem
[...cart, newItem]
cart.concat = newItem
quiz.explanation: The spread syntax expands the existing array into a new array, and newItem is then added as the final element.

exercise.title: Summarize and group a shopping cart
exercise.task: Implement exactly two functions: `summarizeCart(items)` and `groupBy(items, key)`. `summarizeCart(items)` receives items shaped like `{ name, price, quantity }` and returns `{ count, total, mostExpensive }`, where count is the total quantity, total is the sum of price multiplied by quantity rounded to 2 decimals, and mostExpensive is the name of the item with the highest unit price or `null` for an empty cart. `groupBy(items, key)` must return an object whose properties are the distinct `items[key]` values and whose values are arrays containing the matching original items. Neither function may modify the input array or any of its objects; the tests use these exact function names.
exercise.hint: For `summarizeCart`, use reduce to calculate quantity and total, and another reduction to find the item with the highest unit price. Round the total with `Math.round(value * 100) / 100`. For `groupBy`, build a new object and create an array the first time you encounter a key, then push matching items into that array; pushing into the new grouping arrays does not modify the original input array.

tests.name: Summarizes an empty cart
tests.code: const result = summarizeCart([]); return result.count === 0 && result.total === 0 && result.mostExpensive === null;

tests.name: Calculates quantity and total
tests.code: const items = [{ name: "Keyboard", price: 49.99, quantity: 2 }, { name: "Mouse", price: 24.99, quantity: 3 }]; const result = summarizeCart(items); return result.count === 5 && result.total === 174.95;

tests.name: Finds the most expensive unit item
tests.code: const items = [{ name: "Mouse", price: 24.99, quantity: 10 }, { name: "Monitor", price: 199.99, quantity: 1 }, { name: "Cable", price: 9.5, quantity: 20 }]; return summarizeCart(items).mostExpensive === "Monitor";

tests.name: Groups items by a property
tests.code: const items = [{ name: "A", category: "book" }, { name: "B", category: "game" }, { name: "C", category: "book" }]; const groups = groupBy(items, "category"); return Array.isArray(groups.book) && groups.book.length === 2 && groups.book[0] === items[0] && groups.book[1] === items[2] && groups.game.length === 1 && groups.game[0] === items[1];

tests.name: Does not mutate the input
tests.code: const items = [{ name: "A", price: 10, quantity: 2, category: "x" }, { name: "B", price: 20, quantity: 1, category: "y" }]; const original = JSON.stringify(items); summarizeCart(items); groupBy(items, "category"); return JSON.stringify(items) === original;
